title: People in the AI sub - would you play a game if it was AI?
author: re-skob
selftext:
Why do we need 10 of these types of posts here a day? Yes, people in a sub dedicated to AI game development would play a game where AI was used (if it's a good game). They'd play it with AI code, they'd play it with AI art, they'd play it in a park, they'd play it in the dark, yes they would play AI games. If you post the same question to the regular gamedev sub most of them would say no, they wouldn't, if they would they'd be in this sub. So what are you trying to prove by posting this to a sub where the answer is obvious?   
  
This sub has 165k weekly visitors with 13k weekly contributions. The gamedev sub has 456k weekly visitors with 11k contributions, so this sub is almost 3x more active (given the visitor to contribution ratio) and growing significantly faster than the regular gamedev sub, so just make your f'in game and post it and we'll tell you if it's slop or not.

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body: The problem is that game developers spend most their time making games, they aren't a good target market to start with. However yes, if someone made an turnbased AI game, I would slowly play it in window mode while working on my own projects.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: yeah, that's another issue - game developers aren't you're audience, they're a small portion of the gaming market. You're in the market for a windowed turnbased game (AI or not probably), I'm in the market for something else. At the end of the day most gamers just want the game they want and don't care how it's made. People in these subs have a vested interest in the tools that most of the gaming market doesn't.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: I’m ready to mute this sub it’s complaint whining meta posts, I’d like to see actual games and how you use ai to accelerate what you can do and not just do dumb one shot lazy attempts and being in awe of what an llm can do and actually do something.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: it's either crappy one-shots, low-effort AI marketing walls of text, or crabs in a bucket trying to tear down people actively trying to make something good because they're in one of the other 2 categories that outnumber the third

replies.author: MrTheWaffleKing
replies.body:
I've always been more technical than artistic. Being interested in creation thru a technical interface has brought me into these spheres and has shocked me how much that 'crab in a bucket' nature really is true. I mean you see it publicized all the time when artists are shown- public news or movies showing such... it shouldn't have been surprising that people making games for money- who see their peers as competition- act the same way.

It's a different mindset I guess, I make games for fun. I'm not competing with these people.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body:
there is some level of competition - the easier games are to make the harder it is to stand out and with a stagnant consumer base there's the same amount of money potentially divided amongst more projects.   
  
But at the same time other gamedevs aren't your market and the number of people in these subs are a drop in the bucket in comparison to the overall market, so it doesn't make sense to treat people within the community you frequent as competition to be torn down. It's hard enough as is and it's generally better to be positive (but honest) other than being ousted from the community as an a-hole

comments.author: Big-Strategy-5986
comments.body: All that matters is games are fun along of the AAA games look amazing but have no charm and nothing actually fun about the game

comments.author: Varrianda
comments.body: If it was good yes. Majority of AI games are just objectively not good.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: yes, the easier it is to make games, the more inexperienced people make games, but it also allows good devs to make better games so separating the wheat from the chaff is a lot harder

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body:
A better question might be “would you play your own game if you didn’t make it?” It’s surprising how often the answer to that question among beginner devs is “no”. Until you’ve spent a lot of time play testing games with real people it is really easy to see the game you intended to make not the game you actually made. I fairly often answer “what is wrong with my game” posts on Reddit by pointing out really obvious problems that I am sure the poster would see in a heartbeat if it wasn’t their own game.

I think this problem is amplified among people who are making games with AI. It’s all very magical to get a result from a prompt that does a bunch of things you could never have done yourself. That, I think, blinds you to all the stupid decisions the AI made that you wouldn’t have made if you were doing it all yourself. Games made that way often take on what I call the AI smell; they are awkward and ugly in some places and weirdly polished in others resulting in an uneven and sometimes incoherent experience. AI made games don’t have to be that way but, in practice, most of them are.

replies.author: GhamraStudios
replies.body: I agree with this. Here is how I see AI development should go and I am saying this weighing in on my software development career and working heavily with coding AI tools. Prompt -> Game will never be playable and what you want. Here is how developing with AI should be. Prompt -> First iteration -> playtest -> list issues -> repompt and the loop keeps going. With that you also need to make sure you have massive testing for the app to avoid regressions since AI doesn’t check where other things can break unless you have it setup and have the testing in place. I could have said I have a game to publish months ago but every time I playtest I find so many issues that I want fixed or the behavior needs to be different to be more fun. Then I have other people test (friends/family) and I get even more feedback and issues that need to be fixed. This all to say the development cycle has not changed what did is instead of an army of developers you now have an army of agents that are much faster. The core principles are still the same.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body: I find that to be my North Star right now actually. Every decision I make, every step in polishing, is centered around “is this the best I think the game should feel” and “if I were playing this for the first time, is there anything I would say, ‘hmm I kind of pictured it would look better if I just..’”

comments.author: Illustrious-Lime-863
comments.body: I'll play good games like I always have. I don't care how they are made

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: yep, probably the most common viewpoint.

comments.author: Factory-Reset
comments.body: I don't care if AI was used to make it. Ai don't know what's fun, that's on the developer. If it's fun we will play it but most of these AI games are just lazy one prompt copy's. Uninspired, forgettable, boring. Wait for the small teams of passionate artists , story writers, systems designs to leverage AI to bring a dream to life. Coding is the easy part, vision and focus is what matters. And a healthy token budget I suppose lol

comments.author: zayelion
comments.body: If it was good and I had time.

Agreed this sub needs to ban these low effort whining and meta posts or it is destined to be another spam sub everybody mutes.

People who want to argue and complain about pro/anti can go chill in r/aiwars i want to actually learn stuff here.
